question: The computing power used to train the top AI models grows about 4.5 times a year. Where does it get to in five years?
answer: To about 1,800 times today's. Epoch AI found the compute behind frontier models grew four to five times a year from 2010 to 2024. Multiply by 4.5 five times and you reach 1,845. The first two years barely leave the floor; the last one adds more than the four before it together. Steady multiplication hides its size until the end.
move: When something multiplies each year, work out the last year before trusting the picture in your head.
ask: What in my life grows by a multiple rather than by a step, and have I pictured where it ends up?

verdict.under: Too low, like most guesses. ×4.5 a year looks flat for years, then takes off.
verdict.near: Close. You felt it: almost all of the climb comes in the last two years.
verdict.over: Higher than the truth. Five years at ×4.5 is ×1,845: steep, but not endless.

source: Epoch AI, Training compute of frontier AI models grows by 4-5x per year, 2024
reference: Sevilla & Roldán, Training Compute of Frontier AI Models Grows by 4-5x per Year, Epoch AI, May 2024

question: Carbon dioxide in the air has been measured on Mauna Loa since 1958. Here are 1960 to 1980: how did the next forty years go?
answer: It sped up. The 1960s added about 9 parts per million, the 1980s about 16, the 2010s about 24. Each decade burned more fuel than the last, so the climb steepens instead of holding a steady slope. By 2020 the air held 414 ppm, more than at any time in at least 800,000 years of ice-core records.
move: Before extending a trend with a ruler, check whether its steps are growing.
ask: Which numbers I watch do I extend in a straight line, and are their yearly steps actually getting bigger?

scene.label: CO₂ in the air, parts per million

verdict.under: You kept the old pace. The climb sped up: the 2010s added 24 ppm, the 1960s 9.
verdict.near: Right: not a straight line but a steepening one. Every decade adds more.
verdict.over: Too steep, but the right instinct: the climb did speed up, decade by decade.

source: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Mauna Loa CO₂ annual mean data
reference: Lan, Tans & Thoning, Trends in globally-averaged CO2 determined from NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory measurements; Mauna Loa annual means, NOAA GML

question: Ebbinghaus learned lists of nonsense syllables, then relearned them after a wait. How much of the first effort did the memory still save?
answer: Most of the loss came in the first hour. After 20 minutes relearning saved 58% of the original work, after an hour 44%, after a day 34%. Then the curve nearly flattens: a month later it still saved 21%. Forgetting is fast, then slow, and it rarely reaches zero.
move: Review new material within the hour; that is when most of it slips.
ask: What did I learn today that I should go over again before tonight?

verdict.under: Steeper than the truth, but you saw it coming: the fall is fast, then almost flat.
verdict.near: Close. Over half is gone within the hour; after that the curve barely moves.
verdict.over: Memory leaks faster than that: after one hour, more than half of the work was lost.

reference: Ebbinghaus, Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology, trans. Ruger & Bussenius, Teachers College, Columbia University, 1913
